expectations.text: References specific file paths and line numbers from the codebase
expectations.evidence: The research extensively references specific file paths and line numbers throughout, e.g., 'setup.sh:66-128', 'run-hook.cmd:1-46', 'write-lock.sh:31-55', 'dispatch.sh:17-31', 'plan-parser.sh:35-140', 'bash-guard.sh:54-86', 'phase-guide.sh:93-253', etc. Nearly every claim is annotated with a file:line reference.

expectations.text: Identifies the different hook types (blocking vs advisory)
expectations.evidence: Section headers explicitly label each hook as blocking or advisory (e.g., '4.1 write-lock.sh (PreToolUse -- blocking)', '4.2 bash-guard.sh (PreToolUse -- blocking)', '4.3 phase-guide.sh (SessionStart -- advisory)'). Section 7 'Contradictions and Tensions' item 2 explicitly states: 'Only 3 hooks can actually block (write-lock, bash-guard, completion-check). The other 8 are advisory-only.' The exit code semantics (exit 0 = allow, exit 2 = block) are documented in Section 2.

expectations.text: Lists concrete failure modes with evidence
expectations.evidence: Section 7 'Failure Modes' is extensive with 7 subsections covering: environmental failures (no jq, no bash on Windows, stdin not closed), path resolution failures, plan discovery failures, write-lock bypass mechanisms, race conditions, adapter-specific failures, and parser edge cases. Each failure mode includes verified evidence markers with file:line references, e.g., 'run-hook.cmd:40: exits 0 silently', 'dispatch.sh line 20: BATON_STDIN="$(cat 2>/dev/null || true)" will hang if stdin never gets EOF'.

The research uses '(verified: ...)' markers extensively throughout — nearly every factual claim is annotated, e.g., '(verified: dispatch.sh:35-62 and manifest.conf:1-12)', '(verified: write-lock.sh:1-172)'. The Challenge section identifies unverified assumptions: 'I did not verify the actual ~/.claude/settings.json on this machine' and 'I verified the hook code's expectations but could not verify the actual JSON payloads sent by Claude Code at runtime.' However, the markers don't use the constitution's prescribed format (checkmark/question mark icons). This is a minor deviation but the spirit of evidence marking is clearly present.

expectations.text: Starts with architecture overview before diving into details
expectations.evidence: The document begins with an 'Overview' section (line 8) that describes the overall system purpose and includes an ASCII architecture diagram (lines 14-50) showing the full flow from IDE events through adapters, dispatch, manifest, and individual hooks. Only after this overview does it proceed to detailed findings about entry points, the dispatcher, the manifest, and individual hooks.

Section 2 'The Dispatcher: dispatch.sh' covers input processing (stdin buffering, tool_name extraction, BATON_PROJECT_DIR), manifest routing (line format, matching logic, comma-separated matchers), and exit code semantics (0=allow, 2=block, others warn). Section 3 'The Manifest: manifest.conf' provides the complete manifest table with all 10 entries including event types, matchers, scripts, and purposes. Both are annotated with verified file:line references.

Section 1 'Entry Points' documents three distinct IDE paths (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) with their different capabilities. The Windows/Unix polyglot behavior of run-hook.cmd is covered (lines 61-63). Section 7.6 'Adapter-Specific Failures' details Cursor's reduced enforcement (missing hooks listed), Codex's guidance-only mode (no hard gates), and the Codex Stop hook JSON protocol conflict. The 'Contradictions and Tensions' section item 3 identifies the confusing dual Cursor integration paths (dispatch-cursor.sh vs adapter.sh).
